open-question.question: Once the batched shell call makes the Recommendation-annotation and Question-ordering commits itself, from what does the runner learn which of those commits landed, in order to choose between the two success lines and the no-op line of the report step?
open-question.recommendation: The commit facts are read in the same turn from the call that made the commits, with no extra tool call, no git-history read, no per-block ledger across re-sends, and no unstable git summary to scan; a guard that fired prints no marker, so the runner still never tests the sort outcome itself, and the three report lines stay true to the git log.
open-question.alternative: Source: the batched call's own print. Besides its failure lines, the call prints one fixed, identifier-free marker line each time one of its commits lands, one for the Recommendation-annotation commit and one for the Question-ordering commit. It prints the second only when the dirty-own-path guard let the sort's commit through. Git's success output stays silenced. The runner reads the markers across every batch call of the run, re-send calls included, and picks the report line in the existing strict order. The report keeps its three lines. The commit facts come from the same call that made the commits and are read in the same turn, so no extra tool call is needed and no outcome is inferred. A guard that fired leaves no marker, which keeps the step-7 rule that the runner never tests the sort outcome itself. The milestone 43 precedent is a call that prints nothing when everything succeeded, and this departs from it by adding two success-path lines that the call's prose has to define and the runner has to tell apart from failure lines. In a run that writes no block, the reorder line depends on the sort running inside a batch call, which is the axis the "Sort with nothing written" question owns.

Source: git's own output, left visible inside the batched call. The call runs git commit without -q and without capturing its output, so every landed commit prints git's summary line naming its subject, and a guard that fired prints nothing. The runner looks for the Recommendation-annotation and Question-ordering subjects in the combined print of every batch call in the run. The report keeps its three lines. No marker vocabulary of the pass's own is added. The evidence is git's own statement of the commit, so the status line stays tied to the git log, the record its strict order exists to match. The call needs no extra printf. Git's human-readable commit summary is not a stable interface: it includes the branch name and short hash and is followed by file-statistics lines, so the print the runner must scan grows and runs mixed with the call's failure lines. It also reverses milestone 43's choice to silence git's success output.

Source split by commit. The runner infers whether the annotation commit landed from what it already holds: the blocks it sent in each call, minus the blocks the call printed as refused, minus any failed-commit line. A block that went through and committed means the commit landed. Only the sort's commit is reported positively, as one fixed marker line the call prints when that commit lands. Otherwise the call stays failure-only. The report keeps its three lines. The call stays close to milestone 43's silent-on-success shape. The one fact the runner cannot work out for itself, whether the guard let the sort commit through, is the only one the call has to print. Across a first call and its corrected re-sends, the runner has to keep a per-block ledger of what it sent and what each call refused, and an error in that ledger turns into a wrong status line with nothing to check it against. How refused blocks are tied to titles is owned by the "Refused block print pairing" question, and what the tool prints per accepted block is owned by the "Multi-block embed tool form" question. Both bear on how easy the inference is.

Source split by commit, with a closing check modelled on the alternatives pass. After the last batch call, the runner runs list --without-recommendation once. If an id from the step-1c set is missing from that print, the run annotated something, and the runner prints Recommendations embedded. The sort's commit is reported as one fixed marker line the call prints when that commit lands, and the runner reads that marker only when the closing check shows no annotation. Otherwise the call stays failure-only. The report keeps its three lines. The two annotating passes would choose their status lines the same way, from the document as it ends up, and the result holds however many re-send calls the run made, with no per-block bookkeeping. It adds one tool call per run, in a milestone whose purpose is cutting post-decision turns. The check also reads document state rather than git, so an embed that wrote but whose commit git refused still counts as annotated. Only the failed-commit line catches that. The reorder line still needs the call to run the sort in a no-block run, which is the axis the "Sort with nothing written" question owns.

Source: git history, read after the run. Before the first batch call, the runner records the current HEAD commit with git rev-parse HEAD and keeps that one hash as a value. After the last batch call, it runs one path-scoped git log of the subjects committed since that hash to the milestone's open_questions.xml. It picks the report line in the existing strict order from the subjects present. Every batch call stays failure-only and silent on success, as in milestone 43. The report keeps its three lines. The status line is read straight from the git log it must stay true to. That covers every batch call of the run at once, including commits made by re-send calls, and the call script and its print contract stay unchanged. It adds two tool calls per run, one before and one after, and the runner must hold the start hash across calls. That works against the milestone's turn-cutting aim, and it brings a git-history read into a pass that has never needed one.

Rejects the premise that the run must tell all three lines apart. The report step drops the distinction between a reorder and no change: a run with no annotation commit prints one line that says no new recommendations were embedded, whether or not the sort committed. A run with an annotation commit prints Recommendations embedded. The runner needs only the annotation fact, taken from the call's failure-only print and what it sent, and the call carries no sort marker. The CLAUDE.md terse-reporting invariant and the step-7 wording are updated to match. The sort's guard outcome never has to reach the runner, so the batched call stays as silent and simple as milestone 43's and the report step gets shorter. The no-op line no longer promises that the run left git history untouched, since a Question-ordering commit can now land under it. It also changes a recorded invariant, under which recommend-all-open-questions is the one pass with two success lines chosen by what the run committed, for a saving that applies only to runs that write no block.
